lesson.label: Connectivity vs. spatial arrangement
lesson.title: Connectivity vs. spatial arrangement
lesson.tag: Same formula is only the first test

cards.rule: Constitutional isomers share a molecular formula but differ in connectivity. Stereoisomers have the same connectivity and differ in spatial arrangement. Conformers interconvert by rotations about single bonds.
cards.cue: Formula → connections → space. Compare in that order.
cards.trap: A different drawing orientation does not prove isomerism. Rotating the whole molecule changes neither connectivity nor configuration.
cards.app: An alcohol and an ether can share a formula but differ in hydrogen-bond donation, boiling point, and reactivity.

steps.label: 1. Alcohol connectivity
steps.text: Count two carbons, six hydrogens, and one oxygen. The oxygen bears H and can donate a hydrogen bond.

steps.label: 2. Ether connectivity
steps.text: The same formula now has oxygen between two carbons. No O–H bond is present. This is a constitutional isomer, not a different conformation.

steps.label: 3. Branched framework
steps.text: Butane and 2-methylpropane are another constitutional-isomer pair: identical formula, different carbon skeletons.

cards.rule: Angle strain is deviation from preferred bond angles; torsional strain comes from eclipsing bonds; nonbonded (steric) strain comes from crowding of atoms not bonded to each other. Butane anti and gauche conformations are staggered, but gauche has greater methyl–methyl crowding. A cyclohexane chair has nearly ideal angles and staggered bonds; bulky substituents usually prefer equatorial sites to reduce 1,3-diaxial crowding.
cards.cue: For the butane methyl–methyl dihedral shown: anti = 180°, gauche = 60°, ordinary eclipsed = 120°, and totally (fully) eclipsed = 0°. At 0° the methyl groups eclipse one another, giving the highest energy of these conformations.
cards.trap: Axial is not synonymous with up: axial directions alternate. A chair flip swaps axial/equatorial positions while preserving up/down and cis/trans. Boat flagpole contacts are steric interactions; do not call every unfavorable contact angle strain.
cards.app: Conformational preferences affect binding. Cyclobutane puckers and cyclopentane can adopt envelope-like shapes to reduce eclipsing; cyclohexane has higher-energy boat and twist-boat forms, and its chair-flip pathway passes through half-chair transition states.

steps.label: 1. Rotate a single bond
steps.text: Look down the middle C–C bond of butane. Adjust the angle to compare torsional and methyl–methyl interactions.

diagram.caption: Butane viewed along C2–C3: blue front bonds and green rear bonds.

steps.label: 2. Ring constraints
steps.text: This hexagon shows connectivity only, not a flat equilibrium geometry. Cyclohexane normally adopts a chair. An axial substituent interacts with axial groups at C3 and C5; an equatorial position avoids much of this crowding.

steps.label: 3. Ring-flip pathway
steps.text: This hexagon is a connectivity map, not a chair drawing. A chair flip passes through higher-energy shapes: half-chair transition states and twist-boat regions; the boat has flagpole crowding and eclipsing interactions. The final chair exchanges axial/equatorial sites without changing up/down.

lesson.label: Chirality, enantiomers, and meso compounds
lesson.title: Chirality, enantiomers, and meso compounds
lesson.tag: Mirror image ≠ always a different molecule

cards.rule: A tetrahedral carbon with four different substituents is a common stereogenic center. Enantiomers are nonsuperimposable mirror images. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images; E/Z pairs qualify too.
cards.cue: One inverted center in a one-center molecule gives its enantiomer. With several centers, compare the entire molecule.
cards.trap: 2ⁿ is a maximum number of stereoisomers, not a guarantee. Internal symmetry can make a molecule with stereocenters achiral (meso). R/S does not predict the sign of optical rotation.
cards.app: Enantiomers have the same ordinary properties in achiral environments but opposite optical rotations under matched conditions; chiral receptors can distinguish them. A suitable single-enantiomer resolving agent can convert a racemate into diastereomeric salts or derivatives. Their different properties permit separation, followed by regeneration of the original enantiomers. Chiral chromatography is another approach.

steps.label: 1. Identify four groups
steps.text: The alcohol-bearing carbon has OH, H, methyl, and ethyl as four distinct groups. Both carbons of the ethyl group are highlighted. The flat graph does not assign R or S. Try It Yourself removes these walkthrough highlights before asking for an atom selection.

challenge.explanation: Atom B has four different substituents.

steps.label: 2. Count with symmetry
steps.text: Butane-2,3-diol has two potential stereocenters. Its (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) descriptions refer to the same meso compound because of symmetry; the RR and SS forms are an enantiomeric pair. Total: three stereoisomers.

cards.rule:
Rank directly attached atoms by atomic number; isotopes by mass. Resolve ties one sphere at a time using sorted atom lists. Treat multiple bonds with duplicate-atom bookkeeping. With priority 4 away, clockwise 1→2→3 is R and counterclockwise is S.

Absolute configuration assigns a stereochemical arrangement independently (for example R/S). Relative configuration describes a relationship to another stereocenter or reference compound. A remote chemical change can retain the local spatial arrangement while changing CIP priorities and therefore its R/S label; reassess priorities instead of equating a letter change with physical inversion.
cards.cue: Fischer: horizontal bonds come forward; vertical bonds go back. If group 4 is horizontal, reverse the apparent result. We draw C1 at the top here. A 180° rotation of the entire Fischer drawing preserves its configuration.
cards.trap: A 180° in-plane Fischer rotation preserves configuration; a 90° rotation does not. D/L is a relative-configuration convention, not a synonym for R/S or +/−.
cards.app: Most proteinogenic L amino acids are S; L cysteine is R because sulfur changes CIP ranking. Glycine has no stereogenic alpha carbon.

steps.label: 1. Rank the substituents
steps.text: OH ranks first. Ethyl beats methyl at the next sphere: [C,H,H] beats [H,H,H]. The terminal CH₃ carbon of the ethyl group supplies the C that breaks the tie; both carbons of ethyl are highlighted in orange, while the competing methyl carbon is unhighlighted. H ranks fourth.

diagram.caption: Fischer projection of butan-2-ol with C1 at the top. Horizontal bonds point toward you; vertical bonds point away.

steps.label: 2. Orient then assign
steps.text: Use the same Fischer projection with C1 at the top. Priorities are OH (right) > ethyl (bottom) > methyl (top) > H (left). The apparent 1→2→3 order is clockwise; H is horizontal and toward you, so reverse it: S.

diagram.caption: Fischer projection of butan-2-ol with C1 at the top. Horizontal bonds point toward you; vertical bonds point away.

steps.label: 3. Mirror the projection
steps.text: Interchanging H and OH inverts this single center. The mirrored projection is R and represents the enantiomer.

diagram.caption: Mirror Fischer projection with C1 at the top; the horizontal groups are exchanged.

cards.rule: E/Z is defined only if each double-bond carbon has two different substituents. Rank each end by CIP: Z puts the higher-priority groups on the same side; E puts them on opposite sides. E/Z geometry alone does not determine whether a whole molecule is chiral.
cards.cue: Z: higher-priority groups together. E: higher-priority groups opposite. Identify E/Z first, then assess the symmetry of the whole molecule separately.
cards.trap: Cis/trans cannot replace E/Z in every alkene. Both E- and Z-but-2-ene are achiral. Zero optical rotation can arise from an achiral compound or an equal mixture of enantiomers; it does not identify which situation applies.
cards.app: The pure Z isomer of but-2-ene is achiral and shows no ordinary optical activity. It is not a racemate. A racemate requires two distinct enantiomers in equal proportions.

steps.label: 1. Compare the two ends
steps.text: Each alkene carbon bears methyl and H. Methyl outranks H, and the methyl groups lie on opposite sides: E.

steps.label: 2. Same side
steps.text: Both higher-priority methyl groups now lie on the same side: Z. Rotation about C=C would disrupt pi overlap, so these are configurational isomers.

items.label: Compare the winners
items.text: Same side Z; opposite sides E

lesson.label: Optical activity, specific rotation, and resolution
lesson.title: Optical activity, specific rotation, and resolution
lesson.tag: Measure rotation; normalize units; keep configuration labels separate

cards.rule: Observed optical rotation αobs depends on concentration, path length, wavelength, temperature and solvent. In the common solution convention, [α] = αobs/(l × c), with l in dm and c in g/mL. If αobs is in degrees, the corresponding specific-rotation units are °·mL·g⁻¹·dm⁻¹. State wavelength, temperature and solvent when comparing measurements.
cards.cue: 1 dm = 10 cm. Positive (+), dextrorotatory, means clockwise/rightward rotation as viewed by an observer looking toward the light source through the instrument; negative (−), levorotatory, is counterclockwise/leftward. Older texts use lowercase d/l for these signs. Uppercase D/L and R/S describe configuration and do not predict the rotation sign.
cards.trap: Do not put a length in cm directly into a formula requiring dm. Concentration in g per 100 mL needs conversion to g/mL in this convention. A racemate gives zero net rotation under matched ordinary conditions, but zero rotation alone does not prove a racemate. Specific rotation is not just an unnormalized angle.
cards.app: For an ideal mixture of only two enantiomers under matched conditions, ee = |%major − %minor| and observed rotation is the signed enantiomer excess times the pure-enantiomer observed rotation at the same total concentration and path length. A 75:25 mixture has 50% ee; if the major pure enantiomer gives +20°, the mixture gives +10°. These are illustrative practice data.

steps.label: 1. Geometry is not optical sign
steps.text: Butan-2-ol can exist as enantiomers. Its connectivity alone does not specify which enantiomer is present, and an R/S descriptor does not predict (+)/(−). Measure the rotation experimentally.

steps.label: 2. Normalize a measurement
steps.text: Illustrative data: αobs = +1.2°, c = 0.040 g/mL and l = 10 cm = 1.0 dm. Then [α] = +1.2/(0.040 × 1.0) = +30 °·mL·g⁻¹·dm⁻¹. These are practice numbers, not a tabulated value for the displayed connectivity.

steps.label: 3. Resolve a racemate
steps.text: For a suitable substrate, use a single-enantiomer resolving agent to make diastereomeric salts or derivatives. Separate them by a suitable property difference, then regenerate the starting enantiomers. Ordinary achiral distillation does not generally separate enantiomers, which share the same boiling point under achiral conditions.

lessonInventory.coreRule: E/Z is defined only if each double-bond carbon has two different substituents. Rank each end by CIP: Z puts the higher-priority groups on the same side; E puts them on opposite sides. E/Z geometry alone does not determine whether a whole molecule is chiral.

lessonInventory.title: Optical activity, specific rotation, and resolution
lessonInventory.tag: Measure rotation; normalize units; keep configuration labels separate
lessonInventory.coreRule: Observed optical rotation αobs depends on concentration, path length, wavelength, temperature and solvent. In the common solution convention, [α] = αobs/(l × c), with l in dm and c in g/mL. If αobs is in degrees, the corresponding specific-rotation units are °·mL·g⁻¹·dm⁻¹. State wavelength, temperature and solvent when comparing measurements.
